airport.name: Aeropuerto Municipal de Nuevo Casas Grandes

summary: Aeropuerto Municipal de Nuevo Casas Grandes (NCG/MMCG) is a small municipal airport serving the city of Nuevo Casas Grandes in the northern Mexican state of Chihuahua. The airport primarily handles general aviation and limited regional flights, providing the closest air access to the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Paquimé (Casas Grandes), the ancient ruins of a major pre-Columbian trading center. It serves as a convenient gateway for travelers exploring the cultural and historical attractions of northwestern Chihuahua.
faqs:
Q: What airlines fly into Nuevo Casas Grandes Airport?
A: The airport is primarily served by regional and charter operators; scheduled commercial service is very limited, so travelers should check current routes with local carriers.

Q: How far is the airport from the Paquimé archaeological site?
A: Paquimé (Casas Grandes) is located in the town of Casas Grandes, roughly 10-15 km from the city center, with the airport situated on the outskirts of Nuevo Casas Grandes.

Q: Is the airport equipped for night operations?
A: The airport is a small municipal facility with basic infrastructure; pilots and passengers should verify current operating hours and lighting availability before planning evening arrivals.

Q: Can I rent a car at the airport?
A: Rental car services are limited at this small airport, so arranging ground transportation in advance through local hotels or Nuevo Casas Grandes-based agencies is recommended.
transport_tips: Taxis are typically available outside the terminal and are the most common way to reach Nuevo Casas Grandes town center or head to the nearby Paquimé ruins. Having cash on hand in Mexican pesos is advisable, as card payment options at the airport are limited. Visitors planning excursions to the Casas Grandes archaeological zone may want to arrange a hired driver or guided tour through their hotel for convenience.
local_tip: If you're visiting the Paquimé archaeological site, plan your flight to arrive in the morning when the on-site museum and ruins are quieter, and the desert light makes for the best photographs of the ancient adobe structures.
